transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-12 / 16:00 UTC - Duration 52 mins
Attendees: Lily Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Malhotra (CTO - Atlas), Tom Hernandez (Infra Lead - Atlas), Sara Lee (ML Engineer - Atlas)
Summary: Deep dive on autoscaling strategies, burst policies, queueing models, reserved GPUs for Dedicated, impact of KV cache and batching on capacity planning, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run benchmarking and exchange traffic profiles + pricing.

[00:00] Lily: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm lily, AE on the account. marcus is our SE, he'll drive the technical bits. priya/tom/sara, you mind doing quick intros?
[00:12] Priya: yeah, priya here, cto, atlas health. we run patient-facing chat features and some clinical summarization. we've got latency targets ~300ms p95 for short queries and peak QPS can spike.
[00:25] Tom: tom — infra lead. we run on gcp, mostly gke, some on-prem for regulated workloads. we are looking at dedicated capacity for predictable throughput.
[00:36] Sara: sara, ml engineer. working on prompt templates, typical prompt token length 150-400, some long ones to 2k for summaries.
[00:45] Marcus: great. goal today — go deep on autoscaling and capacity planning: burst policies, queueing assumptions, reserved gpu pools, how kv cache and batching change our math, and the on-prem/VPC constraints.

[01:10] Lily: quick sanity check on SLOs — priya you said 300ms p95 for short queries, what's acceptable for the longer summarization flows?
[01:21] Priya: for long ones we can tolerate 2-3 seconds p95, but cost is a concern for heavy nightly batch jobs.

[01:34] Marcus: ok, i'll start with the runtime characteristics. our runtime has continuous batching and kv cache. for many short-turn chat interactions we rely on prefix caching so repeated context is served from kv cache — that reduces compute and latency a lot. but cache hit rate depends on how sticky prompts are.

[01:55] Tom: quick question — does the kv cache live in GPU memory or separate? because on our on-prem nodes memory is tight.
[02:03] Marcus: good question. cache metadata is in host memory, kv cache (key/values) can be either pinned to GPU memory for minimal latency or sharded across host with a GPU fallback. for Dedicated we recommend pinning hot shards to GPU; for private/on-prem we can configure fallback to host-backed kv with slightly higher latency.

[02:30] Priya: and how does that affect autoscaling math? if cache hit drops, i assume we need more GPUs?
[02:39] Marcus: yes. here's a simple queueing model we use: effective service time = base decode time * (1 - cache_hit) + cache_hit * cache_service_time. cache_service_time is much smaller. so if cache hit goes from 70% to 30% your per-request GPU utilization jumps and you need more instances to keep p95 latency.

[03:10] Sara: we usually get ~60% cache hit for chat, but for daily summarizations it's near 0%. so we need mixed workload planning.

[03:20] Marcus: exactly — recommend hybrid pool: reserved GPUs sized for baseline chat load (predictable), with burst capacity for summarizations. burst policy can be either pre-warmed instances or queued requests with graceful degradation.

[03:42] Tom: how does Redwood handle queueing? do you queue on the customer side or at your routing layer? we prefer avoiding long in-cloud queues due to PII concerns.
[03:53] Lily: we have configurable queueing — for Hosted API we have Redwood-managed queuing; for Dedicated and Private you can run the queueing in your VPC. for Private/on-prem we give you the routing component so queues stay in your network.

[04:15] Priya: about burst policies — cost is a concern. what's the tradeoff of keeping reserve idle GPUs vs spinning new ones?
[04:24] Marcus: reserved GPUs give instant capacity and predictable latency but cost more idle spend. spinning ephemeral GPUs saves cost but has startup time (minutes) which can hurt p95. a common policy: reserve enough GPUs for 80-90% of expected peak, then allow cloud-bursting for extreme tails. also use fast pre-warm pools for model warm-up to cut minutes to ~20-30s.

[04:56] Sara: do you support quantized variants to reduce GPU memory and increase throughput?
[05:01] Marcus: yes, we support multiple quantization profiles. int8-like quant reduces memory footprint and can increase throughput but may have quality regressions; we recommend model/benchmark-driven decisions. quantization also changes how many tokens you can pack per GPU which affects batching efficiency.

[05:26] Tom: on batching — is continuous batching automatic and what's the effect on latency?
[05:33] Marcus: continuous batching groups in-flight requests to fill GPU kernels. it improves throughput and lowers cost per token but can add a small delay (micro-batching latency). we give latency SLO knobs: max batch delay, target batch size, and priority queuing for requests that require low latency. for chat you might set max batch delay to 10-20ms; for background jobs you can increase that.

[06:05] Priya: can we set policies per route? e.g., chat route low-latency, summarize route high-throughput quantized.
[06:12] Lily: yes — per-route configs are supported in the console with rollout strategies. you can pin a route to a model variant and batch/quantization profile.

[06:28] Tom: i want to make sure our billing/predictions are accurate. if we have burst spikes of 10x for 5-10 minutes, how should we size?
[06:38] Marcus: two approaches: 1) size reserved pool for steady-state + short-term bursting to cloud with autoscaler that tolerates a ramp-up, 2) implement a queueing policy that allows short bursts to queue (if latency is acceptable) and release concurrency to Dedicated instances. For 10x short spikes, pre-warming a small hot pool reduces ramp. Also look at token-level cost: if bursts are dominated by short chat messages with high cache hit, cost impact is less.

[07:20] Sara: when you say cloud-bursting, is that Redwood-managed or do we need IAM/network peering?
[07:28] Marcus: for Redwood-hosted bursting we handle infra and provide logs. for Dedicated we can set up cross-project bursting that requires peering and IAM. for Private/on-prem there's no Redwood cloud burst unless you opt-in to hybrid mode.

[07:48] Priya: security question — for hybrid bursting where some requests go to Redwood cloud, how is PHI handled?
[07:56] Lily: we have options: 1) avoid sending PHI to Redwood cloud (route PHI to Private), 2) use tokenization/redaction at your edge, or 3) execute under a contractual BAA and encryption-in-transit with KMS. we'll share the compliance docs.

[08:20] Tom: ok, let's talk numbers. our baseline chat steady-state is ~150 qps with average prompt 200 tokens and cache hit 60%. peak can reach 1200 qps for short bursts. want to see a sample capacity plan.

[08:36] Marcus: rough back-of-envelope: assume model decode rps per GPU depends on model family and quant. for a 7B quantized we might do ~80-120 rps for 200-token prompts with 60% cache hit. So 150 qps / 100 rps ~ 1.5 GPUs baseline => round up to 2 reserved. For 1200 qps peak you'd need ~12 GPUs if cache hit stays same; with lower cache hit you might need 2-3x more.

[09:20] Priya: those numbers help. can you provide a spreadsheet with different cache hit scenarios?

[09:25] Lily: yes we'll share a modeler spreadsheet and also run a benchmark against a sample of your prompts.

[09:34] Marcus: benchmarks are important because token distribution and kv cache locality strongly change throughput. we usually run 30-60m jobs that simulate spike patterns and mixed workloads.

[09:48] Tom: for on-prem, we also need to consider GPU packing constraints — multiple tenants on the same host? we prefer dedicated nodes.

[09:57] Marcus: Dedicated supports node isolation: you can reserve GPU nodes for your workloads. we can also do tenant-aware packing to limit co-tenancy. for Private on-prem you'll manage cluster and we provide an operator.

[10:15] Sara: another question — how do you measure and surface cache hit rate and per-route latency?

[10:21] Lily: Console exposes token-level breakdowns, cache hit rates, per-route p95/p99, and per-model utilization. We also emit traces you can ingest.

[10:34] Priya: about quantization QA — what's Redwood's testing approach to avoid regressions?

[10:39] Marcus: we run differential evals on your evaluation prompts and provide quality delta vs baseline. quant profiles are accompanied by per-prompt quality scores and you can set rollback thresholds.

[10:56] Tom: what's the warm-up time for a model when spinning new GPUs? minutes?

[11:02] Marcus: cold start can be several minutes depending on image pulls and model load. we optimize with snapshot images and incremental kernel warm-up; realistic cold starts are 90-180s for large models unless pre-warmed. pre-warm pools reduce that to tens of seconds.

[11:24] Priya: any guidance on autoscaler configs? like scale up/down thresholds?

[11:30] Marcus: we suggest CPU/GPU utilization + request queue depth signals. scale-up: sustained >65-70% GPU utilization or queue depth > N for M seconds. scale-down: <30-40% utilization for a cooldown period. tune cooldown to avoid flapping. Also use predictive autoscaling with traffic forecasting for recurring patterns.

[12:05] Sara: predictive autoscaler — does Redwood provide that or do we run it?

[12:09] Lily: Redwood provides optional autoscaling policies with basic forecasting based on historical patterns; for Private you can bring your own.

[12:20] Tom: we have strong compliance requirements — SAML SSO, audit logs, KMS. any gotchas for Dedicated vs Private?

[12:28] Lily: Dedicated gives you tenancy but control plane is still Redwood-managed; Private puts the control plane in your VPC or on-prem and gives you more direct control over SSO/KMS/Audit. For strict compliance Private is recommended.

[12:45] Priya: for Private on-prem what's the upgrade story? we need strict change windows.

[12:50] Marcus: upgrades are operator-driven; we provide image manifests and upgrade scripts. you can control windows and approve rollouts. canaries are supported.

[13:04] Tom: when sizing hardware for Private, do you provide reference architectures?

[13:09] Lily: yes — we'll share node types, per-model GPU RAM needs, network topology, and storage sizing.

[13:18] Sara: back to queueing models — if we prefer rejecting excess requests vs queuing, how's that configured?

[13:24] Marcus: per-route policy: you can set a hard concurrency cap and choose reject (429) or queue with TTL. also fallback models for degraded capacity are supported. common pattern: low-latency routes = reject; background routes = queue.

[13:44] Priya: about fallback models, do you automatically downgrade to quantized variants or different model families?

[13:50] Marcus: we support automatic policy-based fallback: e.g., try primary model, if capacity not available then route to quantized or smaller model variant. you can set quality thresholds.

[14:05] Tom: curious about metrics — can we export to prometheus?

[14:09] Lily: yes, we have prometheus endpoints and also cloud logging exports.

[14:18] Sara: what about throttling — per-tenant vs per-route?

[14:22] Marcus: both. token-level quotas, per-route concurrency, and per-tenant rate-limits. policies can be hierarchical.

[14:32] Priya: for our traffic pattern, we have daily peak 9am-11am and smaller bursts throughout day. we also have nightly heavy batch summarization. recommended approach?

[14:42] Marcus: keep reserved pool for daytime baseline; create scheduled scaling for predictable windows (9-11am). for nightly batch jobs consider separate high-throughput pool using quantized models and larger batch delays. this keeps cost orthogonal to real-time SLAs.

[15:05] Tom: is there a way to simulate cost under different autoscaling/quantization policies?

[15:11] Lily: yes, our Optimize tool runs cost simulators given token counts, model profiles, and scaling configs. we'll include cost runs in the post-call artifacts.

[15:26] Priya: let's talk SLAs for Dedicated — uptime and latency?

[15:31] Lily: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets depending on tier. we'll detail in the contract.

[15:40] Marcus: want to show a toy example — i'll walk through a capacity table. (screen share)

[16:05] Marcus: example assumptions: model X, 200 token avg, 60% cache hit, per-GPU effective rps 100. baseline 150 qps -> 2 reserved GPUs. peak 1200 -> 12 GPUs. if cache drops to 30% per-gpu rps goes down to ~40 -> need 30 GPUs. big difference.

[16:45] Priya: that's a huge variance. do you have recommendations to keep cache hit stable?

[16:52] Marcus: design prompts to increase locality where possible, use conversation IDs to pin context, and use prefetching for known patterns. also monitor cache evictions and increase hot-shard memory for critical routes.

[17:12] Tom: for on-prem, are there tools to observe per-GPU memory pressure and cache shard placements?

[17:18] Marcus: operator exposes shard map, memory use, and per-shard hit rates. we'll demo in follow-up.

[17:30] Sara: how quickly can we test? we want a benchmark with a sample of our prompts and a mix of chat vs summarize.

[17:36] Lily: we'll coordinate. typical turnaround is 48-72 hours for an initial benchmark with reserved test capacity.

[17:45] Priya: any blockers on our side for the benchmark?

[17:49] Marcus: we just need a representative prompt set and traffic profile (qps timeline + token lengths). also credentials to a small test dataset if PHI, use anonymized samples.

[18:02] Tom: about burst credits or overage — if we go over reserved, is pricing per-minute or per-hour?

[18:09] Lily: overage billing is per-minute of GPU usage for Hosted/Dedicated burst (we bill to the nearest minute). for Private hybrid bursting there are contract specifics. we'll send the pricing matrix.

[18:27] Sara: follow-ups — can you show us an example of an autoscaler config (yaml)?

[18:33] Marcus: yes, we have sample configs. we'll include a recommended starting config tuned to your baseline.

[18:42] Priya: curious on network egress for on-prem -> cloud interactions for hybrid. latency and egress cost concerns.

[18:50] Marcus: hybrid implies cross-network egress; we recommend keeping PHI in Private and non-sensitive workloads in cloud. for egress-sensitive tasks use colocated cloud regions or mirror clusters.

[19:05] Tom: what's the expected ops footprint for Dedicated vs Private?

[19:10] Lily: Dedicated has less ops for you — Redwood manages infra and patches. Private requires more ops ownership but gives control. we have managed services add-on for Private if you want support.

[19:28] Priya: ok, let's confirm next steps and owners.

[19:34] Lily: action items recap — marcus runs a 30-min benchmark with your prompts; lily to send pricing + burst policy doc; tom to share autoscaler settings and traffic profiles. we'll schedule a follow-up after benchmark.

[19:50] Marcus: quick note on testing matrix — we'll vary cache hit (60/30/10%), quant profiles (float16/int8), and request mixes (80/20 chat/summarize).

[20:05] Tom: sounds good. for the on-prem checklist, we'll want node sizing recommendations and the operator manifests.

[20:12] Lily: will do. any other questions?

[20:15] Priya: just one — can we get a short doc on best practices for prompt design to improve cache locality?

[20:22] Marcus: yes, we'll include a short best-practices note.

[20:30] Sara: thanks all.

[20:32] Lily: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with artifacts.

[20:36] Priya: thanks.

[25:06] Marcus: yes, warm pools are region-aware and you can pin pools to regions for locality and compliance.

[40:07] Lily: canary with staged rollout and automatic rollback if error rate or latency regresses beyond thresholds. you can set the thresholds.
